Chapter 8. The Guards: Ordinary People, Extraordinary Cruelty.
When you picture the guards, maybe you imagine faceless agents of terror—those uniformed figures, armed and unyielding. But if you look closer, you'll find people behind those uniforms—each one shaped by their own fears, ambitions, and beliefs.
Some of these guards? They're true believers. They've bought into the ideology that justifies the camp’s existence, holding tight to a story that makes everything seem necessary. Others are just following orders, swept along by a system that rewards obedience and punishes anyone who questions it.
There’s a memory that stands out—a young guard, barely older than the prisoners he oversees. He walks through the barracks with this mix of boredom and unease, barking orders but rarely making eye contact. Sometimes, when the violence gets to be too much, he looks away. But other times, he joins in, eager to prove himself to the people above him. The camp gives him power, and with it, a sense of belonging he’s never felt before.
What’s easy to miss is how incredibly ordinary these guards are. They come from small towns and big cities, from all backgrounds. Sure, some are brutal—they actually take pleasure in what they do. Others are just indifferent, numbed by the routine. And every once in a while, you’ll see a flash of kindness—a guard slipping a prisoner a cigarette, or quietly warning someone before a search. But honestly, those moments are rare exceptions.
The system is set up to make cruelty easy. Orders flow from above, and responsibility is always someone else’s problem. If a guard hesitates, they're quickly replaced. The uniform itself becomes a kind of shield—it lets people do things they'd never imagine in any other setting. Over time, the line between right and wrong just fades away, until the violence starts to feel normal.
After the war, many guards said, “I was just following orders. I didn’t have a choice.” Some of them are haunted by what they did. Others? They feel nothing at all. The real story’s a lot more complicated. What these camps reveal is how ordinary people can become instruments of extraordinary cruelty—not because they’re monsters, but because the system makes it possible. And sometimes, it almost feels inevitable.
When you look back, it becomes painfully clear—the camp’s real power isn’t just in its walls or fences. It’s in the way it turns people against each other, makes cruelty routine, and slowly erases the boundaries of conscience. The guards remind us that the capacity for evil isn’t locked away in a few—it’s a danger that lurks wherever power is left unchecked and empathy fades away.
